hook: You know the line about mercies that are new every morning. But did you know it comes from a poem mourning a burned city?
story:
Before these words were ever sung in a church, they were spoken over ashes.

In the Bible’s own account, the army of Babylon came into Jerusalem, and its captain of the guard “burned the LORD’s house, and the king’s house; and all the houses of Jerusalem”. The walls were broken down all around the city. The people who remained were carried away captive into Babylon. The sources we have call the book of Lamentations a response to that siege and destruction, in 586 BCE.

The poems of Lamentations do not hurry to comfort. The poet of the third chapter begins: “I am the man who has seen affliction by the rod of his wrath.” He says he has been made to dwell “in dark places, as those who have been long dead”. He says that when he calls for help God “shuts out my prayer”. Near the bottom he says what many people in a long grief come to say: “My strength has perished, along with my expectation from the LORD.”

And then, in the middle of it, comes a turn that is easy to miss. “This I recall to my mind; therefore I have hope.” The hope does not come from a change in the circumstances, because the city is still burned. It comes from something the poet chooses to remember. What follows is our verse: “It is because of the LORD’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his mercies don’t fail. They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.”

Notice the small shift in the pronouns. The poem has been “I” for twenty-one verses. At the verse about mercy it becomes “we”. A man who was alone with his suffering says, for a moment, that a whole people is still here.

voices.words: the unfailing faithfulness of a covenant-keeping God

moment:
The poem does not name its poet, and it does not hide where he stands. In the verses before ours he is bowed down: “My soul still remembers them, and is bowed down within me.” In the verses after, the grief has not gone away. A little further on he says, “You have covered yourself with a cloud, so that no prayer can pass through.” Later still, “My eye runs down with streams of water, for the destruction of the daughter of my people.”

So our verse is not spoken from the far side of the pain. It is spoken in the middle of it, by someone who has just said that his hope had perished and who now says that it has a reason after all. He goes on: “The LORD is good to those who wait for him, to the soul who seeks him.” And he adds that grief is not the last word: “though he causes grief, yet he will have compassion”.

The chapter is also built with great care. A Jewish study page notes that it is an acrostic, with three lines for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Whoever wrote it took the time to arrange the sorrow letter by letter. Grief did not end the care for words.
around:
The surrounding chapter moves back and forth. It opens with a long complaint (verses 1 to 20), turns to hope (21 to 33), and then turns again to a call to look at one’s own ways and return: “Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD.” Then the sorrow returns, and the poem closes its third chapter with the cry of someone who has been heard in a dungeon.

The book itself does not end in triumph. Its last chapter asks, “Turn us to yourself, LORD, and we will be turned. Renew our days as of old.” Then its very last verse says, “But you have utterly rejected us. You are very angry against us.” Our verse is a light in the middle of the book. It is not the end of the book.
after:
The Bible says that the exile was not the end. Ezra opens with a king of Persia, and the writer says that “the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia” to send people back to Jerusalem to build the house of the LORD. Years later, in the book of Nehemiah, the city’s broken walls rise again: “So the wall was finished in the twenty-fifth day of Elul, in fifty-two days.” The city that Lamentations mourns was lived in again.

The poems themselves stayed with the people. A Jewish study page tells us that Lamentations is read in the synagogue on the fast day of Tisha B’Av, the day that marks the anniversary of the Temple’s destruction. Each year the community goes back to the ruins in words.

Then, in 1923, the verse found a new home. Thomas Chisholm, a Kentucky-born Methodist minister whose health had forced him out of the pulpit after about a year, wrote the poem that became the hymn Great Is Thy Faithfulness, and sent it to William Runyan, who wrote the tune. According to the United Methodist history, George Beverly Shea sang it at evangelistic meetings in Great Britain in 1954, and it became a favorite. Chisholm himself said it had no special backstory. It grew, he said, from a daily sense of God’s faithfulness. In a letter at age 75 he wrote about his modest income and his poor health in earlier years, and spoke of the faithfulness of a covenant-keeping God.
readings:
Many readers hear the verse as the center of the poem. A grief, a turn, a hope: the bright middle of a dark book. Others stress that the hope does not cancel the lament. An Enter the Bible study says the book makes room for both despair and hope, and the voices of despair are not silenced by the hope of these verses.

A Jewish reading begins from the fall of the Temple and asks why God let it happen. On that reading the book is a theological answer to catastrophe, and the people’s own return to God is part of the picture. The verse is a hinge in a longer act of turning back.

The hymn tradition hears it more personally. For Chisholm the faithfulness was not a single rescue but something he noticed day by day. The three readings do not compete. They answer different questions: what do you say in a ruin, why did it happen, and what does it look like to live with God for a long time.
point: The context shows that this verse was not written from comfort. It was written beside a ruined city by someone who had told God, in plain words, how bad it was. That is why it carries weight: faithfulness here is spoken about a God the poet still addresses after the city has fallen.
lesson:
If you are in a hard stretch right now, this verse does not ask you to talk yourself out of it. The poet did not. He said how dark it was, and he said it for twenty verses. Only then did he say what he remembered.

You can do the same. Say plainly what is wrong. Then ask yourself what you can recall that is true, not what you feel but what you have seen: a kindness, a person who stayed, a day you did not expect to get through and did. The poet’s hope came from remembering, not from the view out of the window.

If you share this faith, you might read the whole third chapter in order, and then pray the way the poem does, from where you actually are. If you do not share it, the passage still offers a way of being honest about pain without being ruled by it. Either way, the invitation is small: begin a new morning with what you do know, and let the rest be open.

echoes.note: Another voice that knew grief says, “Weeping may stay for the night, but joy comes in the morning.” Both texts tie God’s care to the morning.
A psalmist, still in trouble, prays, “Cause me to hear your loving kindness in the morning, for I trust in you.” Like Lamentations, it ties trust to the morning.
Near the end of the same book the people pray, “Turn us to yourself, LORD, and we will be turned. Renew our days as of old.” The hope of chapter 3 becomes a request.
